Now, Nvidia has officially released a statement clearly stating: After multiple rounds of discussions, the Board of Directors has reaffirmed Huang's candor and outstanding leadership abilities. After consulting with senior US government officials, the Board has determined that Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk. This attitude is nothing short of an epic reversal. Previously, US regulatory agencies intervened in the investigation, Nvidia also launched an internal review, and investors even prepared to file a class-action lawsuit. During that darkest hour, Nvidia's board of directors firmly signaled to the outside world that they had no intention of bringing Jensen Huang back. Just when everyone thought Huang's return was hopeless, the ending took a dramatic turn! Now, the board has completely reversed its decision and passed it "unanimously." Harvey Jones, the board chairman who had previously firmly opposed Huang's return, stated: The board believes that Jensen Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and his reinstatement is in the best interests of our shareholders, employees, partners, and customers. We have full confidence in Jensen Huang. Meanwhile, interim CEO Kress has returned to the position of CFO. In his reinstatement statement, Huang thanked everyone in one go—"I am deeply honored to return to Nvidia and lead this globally significant technology company as a new industrial revolution begins. I will shoulder this responsibility with the utmost humility and an even stronger commitment." Finally, 63-year-old Lao Huang said, "I can't wait to get back to work!" Trump's late-night remarks, and the US Treasury Secretary's public change of heart—who exactly caused this sudden shift in public opinion within 48 hours, helping Lao Huang turn the tide? Nvidia's announcement made it very clear—"They listened to the advice of senior U.S. government officials." Clearly, the statements from these high-ranking figures became the heaviest factor in tipping the scales. On November 22nd, Trump posted on social media: He hoped that Nvidia's board would rehire Jensen Huang. This would be the most beneficial option for both Nvidia and the United States.

Then on November 23, Trump went even further, stating that he hoped to see Huang Renxun "officially apologize and then come back."

The truly fascinating part came with an interview with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant.

Then on November 23, Trump stated even more bluntly that he hoped to see Huang Renxun "officially apologize and then come back."

The truly fascinating part came with an interview with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant.

Previously, Bessant had firmly stated that Nvidia "must look for someone outside the company" when searching for a new CEO, and even "needs a major overhaul." At the time, everyone thought Huang was completely out of the picture. However, just a few days later, in a television interview, Bessant replied with a smile: Huang Renxun is now an outsider to the company. Moreover, the reality is that Wall Street only recognizes Jensen Huang. Even though Nvidia just delivered a quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion last week, without Huang at the helm, the stock price still plummeted 14.01% in a single day, marking its worst weekly drop since the 2008 financial crisis. Huang's return has reassured everyone.

Huang's triumphant return, taking only 1 day

In just half a month, we have witnessed the turbulent changes in the American tech industry.

On November 11, Huang Renxun resigned, and the following day the company officially announced that CFO Colette Kress would temporarily take over the company, and Harvey Jones would become chairman. Following this, Silicon Valley tech leaders, Nvidia employees, and shareholders launched a wave of support, with the public petition supporting Huang's return eventually surpassing 200,000 signatures. On November 17th, Huang publicly stated for the first time his willingness to return to the company, but was explicitly rejected by the board. Less than a week later, the situation completely reversed. On November 23rd, the board unanimously voted to approve Huang's return. Kress ended his term as interim CEO but continued as CFO, while Jones remained chairman. From resignation to reinstatement, it took only 12 days. From staunch rejection to unanimous welcome, it took just 6 days. However, Huang's return to the center of power does not mean all the controversies have ended. Nvidia also confirmed that the board's independent investigation will continue. Whether Lao Huang can ultimately land safely remains to be seen, and the story is far from over.

Author: Sleepy

On November 23, 2026, exactly 11 days after leaving the company he founded 33 years ago, Jensen Huang was reinstated.

Nvidia's board of directors issued a statement announcing the immediate reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and director.

Nvidia's board of directors issued a statement announcing the immediate reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and director.

Just six days ago, during the earnings call, facing a quarterly performance of $115.8 billion and a year-on-year increase of 103%, Chairman Harvey Jones told global analysts that the board unanimously accepted his resignation and had no intention of bringing Jensen Huang back. According to reports, at an all-hands meeting on November 18, Jones explained to employees why the board accepted his resignation, using the phrase "not being candid enough." However, in today's announcement, the board stated that after a series of communications and meetings with Jensen Huang, the board was satisfied with his "candor" and his ability to lead Nvidia. In its announcement, the board specifically stated that it consulted with senior U.S. government officials during the decision-making process. The secondary market priced in this change of heart with the most dramatic surge. Following the news of the reinstatement, Nvidia's pre-market stock price rose by approximately 28%, recovering nearly $900 billion in market capitalization in a single morning. After the market opened, the Nasdaq Composite Index rose by as much as 7%, and the S&P 500 rose by 5%. If we shift the focus to other areas, the scene becomes even more intriguing. Just a week before her reinstatement, Cathie Wood, head of ARK Invest, was still continuously reducing her holdings in Nvidia, with the first sale at $156.14; the New York Times had just published a lengthy investigation three days earlier, detailing Jensen Huang's yelling and humiliation of employees within the company; and just a week earlier, US Treasury Secretary Bessenter had on television demanding that the Nvidia board "find a new CEO outside the company," having just invented a completely new set of linguistic definitions in the studio the day before. The ink on the transaction slips was barely dry, and the critical article had only been published for three days, yet the man in the leather jacket had already pushed open the door and returned to his seat of honor. Looking back at this absurd hunt in stages, Beating attempts to understand one question: when a computing power company grows into the foundation of the global industrial revolution, why did the hawks in Washington, the editorial departments in Manhattan, the closed-source giants in Silicon Valley, and the independent directors in Santa Clara all simultaneously have the illusion that they can kick out Jensen Huang? And how was this illusion completely shattered by the evaporation of $2.7 trillion in market value? To understand why Jensen Huang was able to return, we must first understand why he couldn't return at first. What blocked the door was never just the ten independent directors in Santa Clara. The story begins in the Situation Room beneath the West Wing of the White House in Washington, D.C. Over the past year, two distinct lines of thought have emerged within the Trump administration regarding Nvidia and chip exports. One line is Trump's own: business, tariffs, the U.S. stock index—sell chips whenever possible. Trump's attitude towards Jensen Huang was gradually swayed by Huang himself. In July 2025, at an AI summit, he recalled that he initially considered breaking up Nvidia. Last December, it was at Huang's urging that Trump approved the H200 visa, with the U.S. government taking a 25% cut. Commerce Secretary Rutnick was caught in the middle. Hawks felt his regulations were too slow to be implemented; according to the Washington Post, his own reason was that he didn't want a trade war with China. Throughout this controversy, Trump's own stance has remained almost unchanged. At the outset, he told reporters that Jensen Huang was a "very good person" and should continue as CEO. On November 16th, he said he certainly wouldn't mind Huang's return, adding, "I think he's learned a very important lesson." Another line of support is that of the hawks. Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Bessant are two key figures, consistently advocating for tighter controls on chips and arguing that Nvidia's profits shouldn't be prioritized. Huang's stance is self-evident. For years, he has repeatedly lobbied in Washington against stringent export controls, almost always standing in opposition to the hawks. When asked about the divisions within his cabinet, Trump replied, "There are two opinions, two lines of thought." The president himself admitted that his people were not united on this issue. However, the hawks faced a thorny institutional dilemma: in the US government's administrative structure, the authority to approve the Entity List for export controls rested with Lutnick's Department of Commerce. Unable to directly seize control of the Department of Commerce, and unable to convince their own boss, how could they break through this ironclad barrier? In the eyes of the hawks, the turmoil in early November came at just the right time. Someone who had been opposing them for years finally had a reason to be removed. According to a later disclosure by The Washington Post, Rubio made a move that was very characteristic of Washington. He rewrote a departmental assessment report that was originally plainly worded, replacing it with extremely harsh warnings, and created a memo under his supervision for distribution upwards. Immediately afterwards, a large amount of internal material previously locked in administrative files and details of executives' private lives began to flow into *The New York Times*. This was a textbook example of using someone else to do one's dirty work. It's interesting to look at Rubio and Bessant's statements over the past 11 days together. According to reports, when asked about this by reporters on November 8, Rubio said he could not comment, as it was an "internal company matter" for Nvidia. On November 11, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a personal relationship with a subordinate who reported directly to him. That evening, the board accepted his resignation, and on November 12, it was announced that Huang had resigned from all positions. At that moment, the hawks in Washington thought they had won the game. The day after his resignation, Bessant immediately appeared on CNBC and targeted the Department of Commerce. He said that for months, the Treasury Department, the Department of War, the Office of the Trade Representative, and the State Department had all advocated adding the relevant companies to the Entity List, "but the pen is in the hands of the Department of Commerce." Two days later, on Sunday, November 15, Bessant appeared on Fox's "Sunday Morning Futures." According to Fortune, in the same interview, he first praised Nvidia as an excellent company and called Jensen Huang a "highly creative innovator." He then abruptly changed his tune, claiming Nvidia had a "culture of non-compliance," questioning whether the company was promoting these seemingly illegal sales to inflate revenue and profits. He used a bank analogy, saying that if this were a bank, and compliance was done this way, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency would already be involved, and "many executives would be dismissed." Next, he drew a strong red line on personnel: when the board was looking for a new leader, they needed to look outside the company. Looking for a CEO outside the company clearly meant not letting Jensen Huang return, and not letting his people succeed him. However, why did Bessent change his tune just a week later? On November 16, the U.S. Department of Commerce issued a new rule specifically tightening restrictions on remote access to advanced chips. According to The Washington Post, this was driven by the Treasury Department and the National Security Council headed by Rubio. On the same day, Trump, Bessant, and Lutnick flew to Manila on the same plane. On November 17, Nvidia's board of directors established a "National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee" composed of independent directors, specifically to oversee trade compliance. The new rule officially took effect on November 19.

On November 22, 2026, Bessant was interviewed by Face the Nation

By Friday, November 20, when Bessant appeared on CNBC again, his tone was noticeably softer. When asked about the disagreements with the Department of Commerce, he said, "We are all committed to implementing President Trump's directives." ...center">

On November 22, 2026, Bessant was interviewed by Face the Nation

Image source: CBS News

By Friday, November 20, when Bessant appeared on CNBC again, his tone was noticeably softer. When asked about the disagreements with the Department of Commerce, he said He also confirmed that the H200 export policy "continues as planned" because "appropriate controls are in place and remote calls have been contained." On the same day, Trump said at the White House that the United States is a country willing to give people a second chance, and that Jensen Huang had put the US "a full 10 years ahead." More importantly, the same day saw a Black Friday for US stocks. Nvidia's stock plummeted 14.01% in a single day, closing at $125.53, wiping out approximately $2.7 trillion in market capitalization from its October high of $239.24. Putting these events together, the outline of a deal emerges. The hawks got the new remote call rules they wanted, the export control committee on the board, and a compliance mechanism under close scrutiny—all in black and white. What Trump wanted was for H200 to continue being sold, for the US stock market to stop bleeding, and for the person who had put America ahead for 10 years to return to his original position. Having gotten all that, Bessant was able to deliver one of the smoothest political maneuvers in modern history on Sunday, November 22nd, on CBS's "Face the Nation." When pressed by host Margaret Brennan, he first clarified that his statement a week earlier regarding various non-compliance issues at Nvidia was merely a possibility requiring investigation, not a definitive conclusion. He then downplayed the widely publicized personal scandal, calling it "somewhat nonsense" and "a minor flaw of someone." When asked about the president's desire for Huang's return, and his recent suggestion to "look outside," Bessant calmly replied, "I said they should look outside, but Huang is now that outsider." In just one week, Bessant had carefully crafted a way to save face for every statement he made. Meanwhile, Rubio, after senior government officials helped the board make the decision, had not made any public comments on Huang's reinstatement as of press time. On the same day, Trump wrote on Truth Social, "I want the Nvidia board to rehire Jensen Huang. It's the best thing for the company, and for America." The following Monday morning, the Nvidia board unanimously approved the decision. After the reinstatement announcement, Trump posted again, calling it the "right and proper decision." From Bessant's change of heart to Huang's reinstatement, less than 24 hours passed. Once the internal conflicts in Washington were resolved, the return to power was readily available. The perfectly misplaced "Wooden Sister" (a nickname for Huang) is probably the most wronged person in these 11 days. Let's first look at what she did. On September 30th, ARK held approximately 2.56 million Nvidia shares, 85% more than at the end of June. On November 5th, ARK bought approximately $43.7 million worth of shares. On Monday, November 9th, the first trading day after the board announced an investigation into Jensen Huang, while others were selling, ARK was still adding to her position, buying approximately 90,000 shares.

ARK Invest founder Cathie Wood (file photo) Source: ARK Invest, published by TechCrunch

Then, Jensen Huang resigned.

On November 12, the day after Jensen Huang resigned, Cathie Wood was still publicly trying to boost the market's morale using standard Wall Street logic, saying that Nvidia cannot rely solely on Jensen Huang, and even without this co-founder, the company still has an excellent engineering team sufficient to support its future.

From a purely fundamental perspective, there was indeed no reason to sell Nvidia in mid-November. Quarterly revenue doubled to $115.8 billion, net profit was $65.3 billion, and guidance for the next quarter was $130 billion. Based on last Friday's closing market capitalization and a rough annualized calculation of this quarter's net profit, the price-to-earnings ratio was less than 12. However, after Bessant issued an executive threat on Sunday via Fox News, demanding the replacement of executives and a 10-day ultimatum, Bessant couldn't hold out any longer. On Monday, November 16th, ARKK and ARKW funds collectively sold approximately 540,000 Nvidia shares at a loss, worth about $84.8 million based on the closing price of $156.14 that day. On November 19th, she further reduced her Nvidia holdings. On the same day, six funds under ARK acquired 935,000 shares of Anthropic at the offering price of $83, totaling approximately $77.6 million. According to reports, her explanation was that the sale was due to "Huang Renxun's issues." Some have calculated that she sold a total of approximately 710,000 shares in three separate transactions last week, with an average purchase price of approximately $204 and an average selling price of approximately $150. Her logic is actually self-consistent. It is said that when ARK evaluates companies, people, management, and culture are important factors. The founder's departure, coupled with public pressure from the finance minister, results in a deduction in points for this aspect, which necessitates selling—a discipline that has remained unchanged for over a decade. In January 2023, ARKK liquidated its Nvidia holdings, citing overvaluation, missing out on a subsequent tenfold increase, all due to the same set of rules. "Sister Wood understood Nvidia, but she didn't read Washington." This time, the biggest variable determining the stock price was on the table in Washington; Nvidia's financial reports couldn't influence it, nor could ARK's model. The control group was right there. After Huang Renxun resigned, Altimeter and Atreides jointly wrote to the board, asking them not to rule out the possibility of Huang's return; Duan Yongping said he wouldn't sell for the time being on the day Huang resigned, and also sold a lot of put options. Even more typical is Bessant himself. He spent decades on Wall Street as a hedge fund manager, served as the chief investment officer of Soros Fund Management, then started his own firm, Key Square, and later became the Treasury Secretary. A financier who chooses politics can retract his statements within a week, while the market still has to follow his pronouncements. In this era, financiers who don't take a political stance are often short-lived. The New York Times' serialization and the undercurrents in Silicon Valley: If Sister Wood (Huang Renxun) made a mistake in her political maneuvering, then the New York Times and certain people in Silicon Valley genuinely believed that Huang Renxun's era was over. Since the first report on October 29, The New York Times has published no fewer than ten articles about Jensen Huang, at its peak almost one a day, and its flagship podcast "The Daily" even dedicated an episode to him. Their pen traveled from Nvidia's conference room all the way to the White House.

The newspaper logo at the entrance of The New York Times headquarters in Manhattan, New York

Image source: Mark Lennihan/AP

For Washington hawks, feeding the media information was merely a tactical tool to pressure Lutnick and force Nvidia to relinquish compliance and regulatory control; but the editorial department of The New York Times treated this political maneuvering as a historic decisive battle to purge the tech oligarchs.

For Washington hawks, feeding the media information was merely a tactical tool to pressure Lutnick and force Nvidia to relinquish compliance and regulatory control; but The New York Times editorial department treated this political maneuvering as a historic decisive battle to purge the tech oligarchs.

The newspaper logo at the entrance of The New York Times headquarters in Manhattan, New York

Image source: Mark Lennihan/AP

For Washington hawks, feeding the media information was merely a tactical tool to pressure Lutnick and force Nvidia Around the time of the midterm elections, the fear among American progressives and urban white-collar workers about AI replacing mental labor reached its peak. So, when politicians started discussing personal ethics and internal management, these writers immediately launched a frenzy. Around November 11th, columnist Anand Giridharadas published a satirical column in the New York Times opinion section titled "Jensen Huang Betrayed Leather Jacket Enthusiasts," saying that the scandal not only shook Silicon Valley and geopolitics but was also an "earthquake" for leather jacket enthusiasts. The week Huang lost his job, the newspaper's opinion section chose to make fun of his leather jacket. Stephen Witt, who appeared on November 15th, perfectly demonstrated what backstabbing means. As the author of Huang's 2025 biography, *Thinking Machines*, Witt wrote an article in *The New York Times*, claiming that Huang's humble image was a performance, and that he was arrogant and intolerant of dissent. He also brought up an old incident where Huang secretly left a $1,000 tip for a waitress at Danny's restaurant, a fact Witt only found out about after asking the waitress himself. His conclusion was that this was still an act for Huang's own benefit. From November 20th to 22nd, as calls for Huang's reinstatement grew louder, *The New York Times* featured a long article on its front page titled "Threats, Insults, Settlements: How Huang Made Humiliation the Norm," featuring former employees accusing Huang of his abusive language. Beyond the Manhattan newspapers, some within Silicon Valley are secretly anticipating a "world without Jensen Huang." Take, for example, Anthropic, which just completed its $1.4 trillion mega-IPO on November 19th. On the surface, Nvidia is a major investor and the foundation of Anthropic's computing power; but beneath the surface, Jensen Huang and Anthropic founder Dario Amodei have already clashed on two fronts. One is chip exports. Dario Amodei is one of Silicon Valley's most radical regulators, having spent the past year advocating for tighter spending in Washington, directly opposing Huang's lobbying efforts. The other fatal flaw was its business model. Jensen Huang had been wholeheartedly supporting open-source models, from developing Nemotron and investing in Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab to pushing for the acquisition of Hugging Face. For Anthropic, which had built its trillion-dollar valuation on high-priced sales of closed-source models, Huang's downfall was like removing the biggest boulder from its head on the eve of its IPO. Anthropic itself doesn't shy away from this. On the day of its IPO, Daniela Amodei told CNBC that one of Anthropic's unique strengths was its large number of computing power partners, including Nvidia, Amazon, Google, and Broadcom, "which is a helpful strategic advantage for us." In the same interview, CNBC host Andrew Ross Sorkin directly asked Dario and Daniela Amodei, "Nvidia is your investor and participated in this offering, but you're on the opposite side of Jensen Huang on the issue of chips from China. How do you feel about this controversy?" Dario first stated that Nvidia is a long-term partner, then said, "We won't always agree with our partners on policy issues," and Anthropic will continue to stand its ground. Sorkin followed up, asking if they thought Jensen Huang should return. Daniela said, "We obviously won't comment on anything our competitors do." Dario added, "That's Nvidia's decision." A company that received investment from Nvidia referred to Nvidia as a competitor on camera. Whether it was the New York Times' serialization or the cold indifference of closed-source giants, they were all waiting for the same ending: they all thought the Jensen Huang era was over. But reality presented a different story. The New York Times wanted to tell the story of Nvidia employees living in fear, but the open letter titled "Stand With Jensen" garnered over 200,000 signatures in just a few days, including over 10,000 current Nvidia employees. At the all-hands meeting on November 18, employees told CNBC that the prevailing sentiment in the room was the same: they wanted Jensen Huang back. As late as Sunday, November 22, the New York Times was still publishing new follow-up reports. After more than a month of serialization, the grand finale is the return of Consort Xi to the palace. In a palace intrigue drama, the most hardworking performer is often the clown. If this plot seems familiar, that's normal. Silicon Valley CEOs seem to have a particular fondness for returning to the spotlight in November. On Sunday evening, November 20, 2022, Disney announced Bob Iger's return as CEO, replacing his handpicked successor, Bob Chapek. The following day, Disney's stock price rose by more than 6%.

November 19, 2023, Sam Altman

Showing visitor pass upon returning to the OpenAI office

Image source: Sam Altman/X

On Friday, November 17, 2023, the OpenAI board of directors abruptly fired Sam Altman.

On Friday, November 17, 2023, the OpenAI board of directors abruptly fired Sam Altman.

In the following days, over 700 of OpenAI's approximately 770 employees signed a petition demanding the board's resignation and Altman's return. Late on November 21st, OpenAI announced Altman's return, a mere five days later. On November 23rd, 2026, Jensen Huang returned, an eleven-day period. The common thread in these stories is clear: those who were ousted were company icons, the procedures for their removal were legally sound, and their return was due to forces outside the established rules. From Beating's perspective, these eleven days of turmoil delivered a brutally honest demystification of the AI ​​industry, which had been booming for three years. Prior to this, three illusions were prevalent in the business world. The first illusion was that when a tech company grows to a five trillion dollar size, the system becomes more important than people, and any founder is a readily replaceable cog in the machine. The second illusion belonged to the Washington hawks, who believed that administrative pronouncements and compliance pressure could determine who becomes CEO of a company at the very heart of its technological cycle. The third illusion belonged to the Manhattan editorial department, who believed that no fewer than ten articles and commentaries could determine the fate of a business leader in this era. From the day before his resignation until last Friday, Nvidia's market capitalization evaporated by approximately $1.2 trillion, shattering all three illusions simultaneously. In the long period before technological convergence, AI remains a game of the brave, heavily reliant on the intuition of a very small number of leaders. Large companies and sovereign wealth funds, holding massive amounts of capital, are forced to place their bets on a tiny minority capable of defining the next generation of architecture. As for those fund managers who spent the past 11 days scrambling to sell at rock-bottom prices, biographers writing moral eulogies, and politicians who thought they could take over the game with a few juicy revelations, they all probably face the same awkward morning today. At the end of the announcement, Huang Renxun, who had just returned to the palace, said one sentence: "I can't wait to get back to work."

data.title: Developing Intelligent Agents for Enterprises: An Inevitable Path from Tool Upgrades to Organizational Leaps
data.description:
Author: Zhang Feng

I. Why Develop Intelligent Agents? A Soul-Searching Question Amidst the Wave

In the current wave of enterprise digital transformation, intelligent agents are undoubtedly the hottest concept. However, many enterprises, after investing significant resources, often find that the so-called "intelligent agents" are merely smarter chatbots, failing to bring substantial changes to their business beyond occasional "show-off" performances.This inevitably leads us to reflect: What fundamental problem are enterprises trying to solve by investing heavily in developing intelligent agents? Taking the medical device manufacturing industry as an example, this is a typical industry characterized by "high regulation, heavy assets, and long supply chains." A medical device company may have a complete ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning), MES (Manufacturing Execution System), and QMS (Quality Management System), but facing the stringent audits of the FDA or GMP, the data silos between multiple systems, and the compliance verification cycle that often lasts for months, traditional IT architectures often prove inadequate. If intelligent agents are merely adding a "dialog box" on top of these systems, then it is just icing on the cake; the real value lies in the reconstruction of the underlying logic. Developing intelligent agents is not about chasing trends, but about reshaping the core competitiveness of enterprises in the intelligent era. It is an inevitable path from "tool upgrades" to "organizational leaps." II. Value Reconstruction: The "Three Awakenings" of the Intelligent Agent Ecosystem The fundamental purpose of enterprises developing intelligent agents is to achieve a deep "awakening" in three dimensions. 1. Awakening Dormant Data and Reshaping Agile Governance (For Business Sector) In the medical device industry, data is the lifeblood of enterprises, but it is often also a heavy "historical burden." Raw material input in production, channel sales in distribution, and inspection records in quality control are often scattered across different systems, forming "siloed" data islands. The KPI reports seen by management are often "second-hand data" that has undergone multiple layers of processing, resulting in delays and distortions. The core value of intelligent agents lies in becoming the "meta-hub" of an enterprise. It doesn't require fundamental modifications to existing systems, but rather uses a non-intrusive approach to connect all business systems, transforming static, dormant historical data into schedulable and analyzable core production factors. When market demands change or regulatory policies adjust, intelligent agents can rapidly orchestrate underlying data capabilities, achieving minute-level restructuring of business processes, truly empowering enterprises with "agile governance" capabilities. 2. Awakening Human-Machine Collaboration and Coordinating Compliance Operations (For Governance) The medical device industry has a saying that "compliance is life." From UDI (Unique Device Identifier) ​​coding to GSP (Good Supply Practice) traceability, compliance requirements permeate the entire product lifecycle. In the traditional model, employees spend a significant amount of time on tedious document verification, ledger generation, and cross-system data transfer, which is not only inefficient but also creates the potential for human error. The introduction of intelligent agents has completely changed this situation. They can take over those tedious, repetitive, and standardized execution tasks, freeing human employees from inefficient labor and allowing them to return to decision-making positions that require more creativity and judgment. More importantly, intelligent agents, through their design of full-link operation traceability and full-process auditability and traceability, perfectly align with corporate compliance requirements. They achieve "operation within compliance, and compliance within operation," making every decision traceable and every execution rock-solid. 3. Awakening Organizational Evolution and Accumulating Practical Experience (For the Organizational Level) The core competitiveness of an enterprise is often held by a few senior experts. In medical device R&D and manufacturing, the experience of a senior engineer and the regulatory acumen of a quality expert are valuable intangible assets for a company. However, this tacit knowledge is often difficult to replicate, and once talent is lost, organizational capabilities will suffer a break. Intelligent agents can "distill" and solidify the operational processes, decision-making logic, and business experience of these outstanding employees into standardized digital assets. These assets are not lost due to employee departures; instead, they continuously iterate themselves through ongoing human-computer interaction. Intelligent agents create a "digital brain" that never leaves, upgrading organizational capabilities from "relying on individual core employees" to "relying on the continuous evolution of the central system." III. Linkage Mechanism: How Intelligent Agents Become a "Three-in-One" Super Hub These three "awakenings" do not exist in isolation but form a positive-cycle flywheel through intelligent agents. Data-Driven Collaboration: High-quality data development and utilization provide intelligent agents with precise "ammunition." For example, in Intco Medical's practice, by building a "cloud-edge-device" collaborative industrial internet platform, intelligent agents can access production data in real time, achieving millisecond-level visual inspection and reducing the product miss rate to below 0.3%. Collaborative Experience Accumulation: In the process of human-machine collaboration, excellent human decisions and the execution data of intelligent agents are continuously recorded and accumulated. For example, in the order review process, intelligent agents use large-scale model reasoning capabilities to automatically compare artwork and orders, reducing the review cycle from days to hours. These efficient processing logics are then transformed into organizational knowledge assets. Experience feeds back into data: The accumulated organizational experience, in turn, enriches the data foundation, enhances the capabilities of intelligent agents, and thus initiates the next round of higher-level collaboration and evolution. Intelligent agents are not isolated tools, but rather "service hubs" that connect data, empower humans, and reshape organizations. IV. Implementation Path: From "Scenario Solving" to "Ecosystem Building" So, how exactly should enterprises develop intelligent agents? Based on our experience in the medical device industry, we recommend following a four-step approach: Step 1: Focus on business challenges and identify the right entry point. Reject "AI for AI's sake." Companies should start with their core processes that determine their success or failure, identifying the areas most critical to financial performance and organizational health. For example, to address the pressure of unannounced inspections commonly faced by medical device companies, priority can be given to developing "compliance self-inspection agents" to automatically identify regulatory updates and alert on risks. Step 2: Build a solid foundation based on data development and utilization. The quality of the agent's recommendations highly depends on a strong data governance foundation. Companies need to unify basic objects and indicator definitions to establish a high-quality data governance system. For example, in the R&D phase, agents can break down data barriers between R&D and production, ensuring that design changes are synchronized to the production line in real time, avoiding the mixing of old and new versions. Step 3: Use multi-layered value alignment as a safeguard to ensure controllability. data.title: A historic record was set overnight: Jensen Huang's return to the company triggered a surge in Nvidia's stock price.
data.description:
Author: Xiao Yanyan, Jinshi Data

US President Trump's push for Jensen Huang to return to Nvidia (NVDA.O) not only helped the AI ​​chip giant achieve a significant stock price rebound, but also allowed Trump himself to reap substantial paper profits from his stock investments.

Nvidia's stock price closed up 31.5% on Monday, marking its largest single-day gain since May 2023. According to an analysis by the Financial Times, this rebound added $952 billion to the company's market capitalization, setting a new record for the largest single-day increase in market capitalization for a listed company globally.

Meanwhile, the market value of Trump's Nvidia shares increased by approximately $15 million.

Financial documents disclosed by the U.S. government show that as of September 30, Trump may have held as many as 370,000 shares of Nvidia stock. This stock price reversal occurred after Huang Renxun was reinstated. Previously, controversies surrounding his personal relationships and market concerns about the sustainability of the AI ​​investment boom had put pressure on Nvidia's stock price. Trump not only publicly supported Huang but also personally pushed the board to change its previous decision. Nvidia announced on Monday that, after a series of discussions and meetings, the board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as CEO. The board stated that, after reassessment, it was satisfied with Huang's candor and ability to lead the company. Less than two weeks ago, Huang resigned as CEO of the world's leading AI chip company. Following Huang's departure, Nvidia's stock price was sold off, and its partners and customers in the technology industry were also affected. Trump, however, has consistently supported this AI industry leader and wanted him to return to the company. Huang responded to the reinstatement. He stated that he was "honored to return" to the company he co-founded 33 years ago, adding, "I will take on this responsibility with the utmost humility and a renewed sense of responsibility." Later Monday evening, Huang returned to Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, where he was greeted with applause from employees. Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones stated that restoring Huang to his position was in "the best interests of shareholders, employees, partners, and customers." On the same day, U.S. stocks also saw a strong rebound. The S&P 500 closed up 4.7%, and the Nasdaq 100 rose 6.9%. However, despite a 31.5% surge in its stock price, Nvidia's shares are still about 5% lower than their level on November 11th, before Huang's resignation. Trump's book profits, estimated at up to 370,000 shares, come from his previous holdings of Nvidia stock. According to financial disclosures filed with the U.S. Office of Government Ethics, as of September 30, he may have held up to 370,000 Nvidia shares. The latest disclosure was filed on November 5. However, these documents do not disclose the exact number of shares held, nor do they provide precise records of each stock transaction; they only list a broad range of holdings. The disclosures only cover investments up to the end of September and do not reflect Trump's stock transactions during October and November. Therefore, the actual size of Trump's holdings needs to be estimated using different assumptions.

Based on the calculation method for higher shareholdings, assuming Trump buys the maximum quantity within the declared range each time and sells only the minimum quantity each time, then his holdings of Nvidia stock at the time of the latest financial disclosure could reach a maximum of 370,000 shares.

Based on this holding limit, after Monday's 31.5% stock price surge, the book value of Trump's Nvidia stock could increase by approximately $15 million.

However, if we use another calculation method, assuming Trump sells the maximum number of shares each time he sells and buys the minimum number each time he buys, then his holdings might only be about 32,000 shares, worth about $5.3 million. In this case, the book profit from Monday's stock price increase would be about $1.3 million. The significant difference between the two estimates reflects that the publicly disclosed documents did not provide sufficient detailed transaction information to determine Trump's actual shareholding and profit. Previously, Nvidia's stock price had been under continuous pressure. If we estimate based on the maximum holding limit of 370,000 shares, before Monday's rebound, the market value of Trump's related holdings had already lost about $42 million from its previous high. Trump's portfolio employs a strategy of buying a broad portfolio of stocks that represent the S&P 500 index. Nvidia is one of the largest companies by market capitalization in the S&P 500. The White House did not respond to requests for comment regarding Trump's Nvidia holdings and his book profits. However, Trump's stock gains have already drawn attention from Democratic lawmakers. Senator Ruben Gallego, a Democrat from Arizona, posted on social media: "We need to investigate what stock transactions occurred before this announcement. This White House is the most corrupt administration in American history."

data.title: Grayscale: Crypto Asset Oversold, AI Risk Remains a Core Variable
data.description:
Author: Zach Pandl, Head of Research at Grayscale; Translated by Shaw, Jinse Finance

The crypto market experienced significant volatility last week. We believe that Bitcoin and other major crypto assets have entered oversold territory, but the short-term market outlook will be determined more by AI-related risks than by blockchain fundamentals.

On Saturday, November 21, the price of Bitcoin fell to $55,000, breaking below the previous low of $58,000 reached on June 30.

This bear market thus became the longest in history (at least 411 days), but also one with a relatively mild decline, with a maximum drawdown of 56% (Figure 1). Bitcoin subsequently experienced a partial recovery, and at the time of writing, the price was approximately $62,000. [Figure 1: Bitcoin's longest and relatively smallest bear market in history] Price signals and money flow indicators both showed the market was oversold. Last week, global cryptocurrency exchange-traded products (ETPs) saw outflows exceeding $2 billion, with stablecoins experiencing large-scale redemptions; Bitcoin and Ethereum futures open interest fell to summer lows; in the options market, implied volatility curves were deeply inverted, with investors paying high premiums for put options (Figure 2). We believe that the fundamentals of public blockchains remain robust, and for investors holding positions for the medium to long term, current valuations offer good investment opportunities. However, the short-term risks of AI-related assets remain high. Since the beginning of November, a series of events are worth noting: (1) The midterm election results may affect data center construction; (2) Jensen Huang was once dismissed, but later returned to serve as CEO of Nvidia; (3) Service interruptions occurred at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft Outlook, several large financial institutions and the National Security Agency (NSA); (4) Anthropic completed one of the largest IPOs in history; (5) It was reported that Claude solved the Riemann Hypothesis - a problem related to the distribution of prime numbers that has plagued the mathematical community for nearly 170 years. The Grayscale research team is very optimistic about the productivity improvements that AI is expected to bring, and also optimistic about the important role that public chains can play in the AI-centric financial system. However, short-term uncertainty remains high, and we advise investors to focus on a long-term perspective when allocating digital assets. **Key Conclusion:** In our view, the crypto market is oversold, with a positive long-term fundamental trend. However, short-term market movements depend on various uncertainties within the AI ​​sector.

data.title: Trump's one-hour interview reveals the inside story of Lao Huang's return.
data.description: <div class="share___SVvtl"><div>On the morning of November 23, shortly after Nvidia announced Jensen Huang's reinstatement, Trump called into CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" for a nearly hour-long interview. This interview revealed many previously unknown details, including how Trump persuaded the Nvidia board, why he insisted on bringing Huang back, how he discussed Huang with Chinese leaders during his visit to China, and his views on the export control and espionage controversies surrounding Huang. The CNBC reporter asked Trump what happened over the weekend and why the Nvidia board's attitude suddenly changed so drastically. Trump stated that he has always firmly believed Huang should return, and this belief has only grown stronger as Nvidia's situation has worsened. He has been communicating directly and indirectly with the Nvidia board and has also spoken with many business leaders. Several people within the government were also involved, with Trump specifically praising Vice President Vance, Treasury Secretary Bessant, and Commerce Secretary Lutnick. One of the Nvidia board's primary concerns was whether Huang's return would pose a national security risk. Trump said the US government had been investigating for weeks, not just in the last day or two. After extensive investigation, the government informed the board that no such issue existed. The board ultimately made its decision in accordance with the Trump administration's wishes. CNBC host David Faber revealed that until the latter half of last week, he had spoken with some people close to the Nvidia board of directors, who told him very confidently that Jensen Huang would absolutely not return, even using profanity to emphasize this point. So, what exactly did Trump say to the board that made them change their minds? Trump's answer was straightforward: "I talked to them, I convinced them." Trump also said that convincing the board yesterday was much easier than a week and a half ago. A week and a half ago, the company's stock price was still high, and some people felt they were about to take over this amazing company, which was naturally exciting. But when the company's stock price started to fall by 40% or even 50%, they found that the job wasn't so easy after all. So, persuading them yesterday was much easier. Previously, he mainly communicated with the board through representatives, not directly intervening as he did yesterday. When pressed by reporters about whether Trump directly called into the Nvidia board meeting, Trump didn't answer directly, only saying he had representatives at the board, but refusing to disclose who he spoke with. When asked if Huang could have been reinstated without his intervention, Trump clearly replied, "No." He considered his involvement crucial. However, Trump doesn't support holding the Nvidia board accountable or demanding their removal. He said the board was initially placed in a very difficult position and didn't have as much information as the government does now. Perhaps a better approach would have been to give Huang a temporary leave of absence instead of forcing him to resign. But it took courage for the board to ultimately change its mind. He saw it as a disaster if the board insisted on confronting the government. Trump also revealed that after everything was settled last night, he called Huang. He didn't discuss corporate governance or make any other specific demands, only asking Huang to promise him one thing: to work hard. Trump told him, "You have the brains and all the qualifications. As long as you work hard, no one can beat you." Huang replied that he would work harder than ever before. Trump said Huang was very excited at the time. II. Why did Trump insist on bringing Huang back? CNBC asked Trump if last week's sharp drop in tech stocks influenced his decision to reinstate Nvidia. Trump admitted that it might have been a factor, but he valued the long-term impact more. Trump said that Nvidia has many chip designs in mind that others don't know or understand, including himself. Nvidia is already thinking about the next three generations of chips, while others haven't even reached that stage. Blackwell will eventually become obsolete, but Nvidia already has ideas far more advanced than Blackwell's. Trump spent a long time explaining why chips are different from other commodities. He said he has a friend who makes car floor mats, and as soon as the product comes out, it's quickly copied by other companies; another friend makes movies, and within 24 hours of the movie's release, millions of pirated copies appear worldwide. But the most advanced chips are different. Even if others get the product, they don't have the ability to replicate it because they don't have the technology or the mindset. He once specifically asked Huang why others couldn't copy his chips like they copied other products. Huang told him it was because others couldn't. Trump believes that Nvidia now has a very high technological starting point and can continue to move forward based on Blackwell. And Huang is the person who understands this technological foundation best and knows best where to go next. CNBC's Jim Cramer called Huang a "national treasure" of America. Trump really liked this analogy, even joking that he would use it from now on without crediting Cramer. Trump repeatedly emphasized that America doesn't have that many geniuses and that these people must be protected. He also mentioned that he protected Musk during his first term, and that Musk might not be where he is today without his help. Of course, the stock market performance is also something Trump cares about very much. During the interview, Trump kept watching the stock price movements on the CNBC screen. He said that Nvidia's stock price was like a rocket flying in the wrong direction, but now it's finally flying in the right direction, and it's lifting the entire market. Trump compared the American AI industry to a baseball team with ten star players, but if one superstar is suddenly ejected, the entire team's performance will be affected. Huang's departure not only affected the stock market, but in his view, it even influenced the outside world's perception of the United States. When CNBC asked him if he was worried about an AI bubble, Trump said he wasn't worried anymore because one of America's most important star players had returned to the court. III. Discussions between Trump and the Chinese side regarding Huang during Trump's visit to China. This is a very noteworthy part of the entire interview. Trump repeatedly mentioned that his recent trip to China was also a factor that prompted his firm support for Huang's reinstatement. Trump revealed that he spent a considerable amount of time discussing Huang with the Chinese side. To Trump's surprise, the Chinese side spoke very highly of Huang's technical abilities, calling him a very intelligent person, and showing him a level of respect exceeding that for most people. This raised a concern for Trump: if the US no longer wanted Huang, would China poach him? Trump said that after returning from China, he considered that China might very well spend a large sum of money to invite Huang to manage a company in China. If Huang was angry about the treatment he received in the US, would he simply go to China? Blackwell's technology was in his mind; it was his own child, and no one understood the technology better than him. Trump even directly mentioned Huawei. He imagined that China could simply ask Huang, "Would you be willing to come to China and lead Huawei, or lead another company of ours?" If Huang is truly disappointed with the US due to unfair treatment, who can guarantee that such a thing will never happen? A CNBC reporter immediately followed up, asking if Trump received any indication during his time in China that China actually intended to do so. Trump clearly answered no, not even a hint. He only made that connection based on the high regard the Chinese side had for Huang. Huang himself never expressed any intention to go to China to him. But Trump said that if he were in China's position, he might have done so. He even told several people around him that he knew what China might be thinking, because if he were in Huang's shoes, he would think: why not just make a deal with Huang directly? This way, there's no need for spies; just invite Lao Huang over. Trump later half-jokingly said that if he were Chinese, he would immediately invite Lao Huang to China, giving him whatever he wanted, even the entire city of Beijing. Regarding whether Lao Huang violated US chip export controls, Trump said the Department of Justice had conducted a thorough investigation, and investigators believed Lao Huang could be cleared of suspicion. Trump's basic logic is that Lao Huang is in the chip business. If Nvidia sells chips to a company, and that company later resells those chips to China, then the responsibility should first be investigated against that company, not automatically attributed to Alice Huang. If someone sells chips to China that shouldn't be sold to China, the president would naturally be unhappy, but the government's current strong assessment is that Huang herself was unaware of these matters. Why would Huang take such a big risk? However, Trump admitted in an interview that he didn't even know if the transaction actually occurred or what kind of chips were sold, and what kind of chips were sold is a very important question. Regarding Alice Huang's alleged contact with Chinese intelligence personnel, a CNBC reporter, citing a New York Times report, asked Trump if this didn't concern him about national security risks. Trump's first reaction was: "Who hasn't been in contact? I just returned from China and met with the Chinese side. The Chinese have contact with many people, including me; that doesn't prove anything." The reporter then followed up, asking if Trump thought there was nothing wrong with Alice Huang's contact with Chinese national security personnel. Trump again joked about his own meetings with the Chinese, saying that if that logic applied, wouldn't he be implicated as well? Now, every time a beautiful Chinese woman appears, someone says she's a spy. But in the case of Alice Huang, I don't believe that's true. CNBC host Sara Eisen specifically asked Trump if he had directly asked the Chinese side whether Alice Huang was a spy during his time in China. Trump replied, "No, I didn't discuss that with the Chinese side, nor did I discuss such specific details." Eisen then followed up: Was the assessment that Huang did not pose a threat to national security Trump's own, or the assessment of the US national security team and intelligence community? Trump replied, "Both. The relevant personnel provided me with their assessment; they certainly have more information than I do. But from day one, I felt Huang was innocent." If I believed that Huang had actually done anything illegal, I wouldn't have recommended his reinstatement to the board. Reporters repeatedly tried to press Trump about what information the CIA had provided, but Trump consistently refused to disclose specifics, only stating that he had received the necessary confirmation and, without such confirmation, he wouldn't have facilitated Huang's reinstatement. Reporters also asked if Trump had assured the Nvidia board that Huang wouldn't face criminal charges related to export controls. Trump didn't explicitly make such a promise, only reiterating that the government believed Huang was innocent and that he had indeed provided assurances to the board. However, he also acknowledged that such assurances could only be based on the information the government currently possessed. V. How Does Trump View Chip Export Controls to China Now? A CNBC reporter presented Trump with two opposing viewpoints within the US regarding chip export controls. One, held by Huang, argued that the US should continue selling chips to China, allowing China to rely on the US chip and technology ecosystem, rather than forcing China to build its own chip industry. The other, held by China hawks, argued that the US should not enhance China's AI capabilities by selling advanced chips. When asked which viewpoint Trump currently agrees with, Trump replied that he understands Huang's logic. If the US doesn't sell, China will manufacture its own. China already has some very impressive companies, and in many chip technologies, China is not far behind the US. For chips whose technology is relatively outdated and which China can produce itself, there's no need to be overly concerned about selling them to China. Trump mentioned the H200 in an interview, saying that such chips are already semi-obsolete and China has its own similar products. However, Blackwell and other state-of-the-art chips are a different story, because these chips cannot currently be replicated by other countries. Chip technology iterates very quickly; today's most advanced chips may be obsolete in a year or two. Even when Blackwell becomes obsolete, he wouldn't object to selling it on the market, because by then, China may already have its own similar products. Sixth, why does the US president intervene in the internal governance of a listed company? Are there any boundaries to this intervention? CNBC host Sara Eisen asked Trump a pointed question: Why would the US president intervene in the internal governance of a publicly traded company and decide who should manage it? Where exactly are the boundaries of this intervention? Trump acknowledged it was a good question, but his answer was that he was doing so in the national interest. He felt compelled to intervene after seeing the US stock market lose $5 trillion in market capitalization following the midterm elections. He argued that without his intervention, Nvidia might have struggled for a long time, even slowly declining. He had seen many such companies before, and some very talented CEOs who were ousted due to personal scandals, only to have the board replace them with far less capable individuals, resulting in companies failing to recover for ten or fifteen years. But Huang's case was more unique than typical corporate executive scandals because of the crucial knowledge he possessed. CNBC pressed further, asking, "Since Nvidia can be considered a national strategic enterprise for the United States, what about Microsoft? Google? OpenAI and Anthropic? If these companies encounter similar problems in the future, will Trump intervene directly?" Trump replied that there's no fixed formula for this; it requires intuition and judgment. Like a skilled golfer hitting the ball near the green, some know how to hit the ball perfectly, while others don't. It must be judged on a case-by-case basis. He certainly wishes there were a formula, but there isn't. Huang's case is one he felt very strongly about; he believes the US cannot lose this person. He has also helped Musk and other entrepreneurs before, and these kinds of situations require specific analysis. He later added, "I manage America, not Nvidia. But Nvidia is a very important part of America." VII. How does Trump view Nvidia's personal issues, and whether corporate governance needs to be changed after his reinstatement? A CNBC reporter asked Trump, "Nvidia has lost a considerable amount of credibility because of this scandal, including media reports of his inappropriate relationships with subordinates. After regaining control of Nvidia, he will likely need to put in a lot of effort to rebuild his authority. What is Trump's opinion?" Trump's assessment was exactly the opposite. He believes that Huang's return might even be more motivated than before, and his personal position might not necessarily be weakened. Huang did make a serious misjudgment regarding personal matters, but this was primarily outside of company business. Huang has apologized to the company, the country, and his family. Trump has also repeatedly mentioned Huang's wife, praising her support throughout the process. Trump even believes that this controversy might ultimately have some positive effects. While Nvidia has been placed under a very negative spotlight, it is precisely this controversy that has made many people realize just how advanced Nvidia's technology is and how important Huang himself is to the company. Jim Cramer then asked Trump whether Nvidia's corporate governance should also be changed. For example, are there too many people reporting directly to Huang? Has Trump asked Huang to correct certain practices or make any assurances to the board? Trump said that when he called Huang last night, he didn't discuss these issues. He believes Huang knows what he should and shouldn't do, even better than they do. His only requirement is for Huang to work hard. When asked if this meant Huang was "too big to fail," Trump rejected the notion, saying only that Huang is a very smart person and the US wants him on his side. The CNBC host mentioned that just a few weeks ago, Trump publicly suggested that Apple CEO Tim Cook take over Nvidia. What's the story behind this? Trump explained that the Nvidia board made it very clear that Jensen Huang would not be returning, and he was surprised by the board's firm stance. Since Huang's return seemed impossible, he considered Tim Cook. He greatly admired Cook, believed he had done an excellent job at Apple, and trusted Cook's ability to manage Nvidia. However, Nvidia's situation was different from Apple's. Chips are extremely complex technological products, involving the future direction of technological development. At this level, he believed no one could do what Huang had done. Trump also believed that if Cook took over Nvidia, he could help the company's stock price recover, but he doubted anyone could achieve such a significant rebound in Nvidia's stock price in such a short period as Huang. 8. Did Trump consider allowing the US government to invest in Nvidia? CNBC host Carl Quintanilla asked Trump if he had considered having the US government take a stake in Nvidia during the process, or if he still had such thoughts. Trump joked that he would certainly be happy to, but didn't want to be prosecuted for insider trading. He added that it would be interesting to have the US Department of Justice sue the US government for insider trading. Trump then said that when he facilitated Nvidia's reinstatement, he didn't know how the market would react. While he thought a stock price drop was unlikely, anything could happen in the market, and he hadn't anticipated such a strong reaction. He emphasized that he wasn't considering profiting from government investment at the time; his primary consideration was the importance of this matter to the United States. Near the end of the interview, CNBC asked whether the US government would intervene to support Nvidia if these financing arrangements encountered problems, given that Nvidia has supported numerous AI companies through various investments and financing arrangements. Trump stated that he did not believe this would happen. He added that Nvidia's chip demand is extremely high, not only for current chips but also for future chips yet to be released. He emphasized the company's strength. (nine questions follow: What does Trump think of those within the Republican Party who oppose Nvidia's reinstatement?) A CNBC reporter asked Trump what he had to say to several Republican members of Congress, including some national security and China hawks within the government, who were concerned about Huang's reinstatement. Trump appeared unconcerned. He said things would be better after he spoke with them, and that they were all good people. However, Trump also took the opportunity to criticize three or four Republicans he believed had previously obstructed legislation, saying their actions were one of the reasons for the Republicans' poor performance in the midterm elections. He did not name them or specify how he planned to persuade the Republicans opposing Huang's reinstatement. The reporter then confirmed whether Trump believed Republicans would ultimately accept the decision. Trump replied that they would. X. Other Questions Regarding OpenAI, Anthropic, and AI Security. CNBC asked Trump that some people within OpenAI and Anthropic are concerned that AI technology is developing too rapidly and could pose serious security risks to humanity. If Trump believes these companies are developing too quickly, would he intervene in these companies as he did with Nvidia? Trump replied that the Department of Justice would intervene. He then spoke about Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, saying he didn't know Dario before and, based on descriptions, thought he was Darth Vader from Star Wars. But after meeting him, he found Dario to be a very good and intelligent person. Trump believes that dealing with such geniuses sometimes requires patience, just as the best Broadway actors are often more difficult to work with than ordinary actors. Regarding TSMC and US chip manufacturing, Trump also mentioned TSMC Chairman C.C. Wei, praising him as a very remarkable genius. Trump said that it was precisely because of his tariff policies that TSMC was willing to spend hundreds of billions of dollars to build factories in the US. He also mentioned potential new projects in Texas, claiming that imported chips could face a 200% tariff in two years, which is why these companies are now building factories in the US. If he announced the cancellation of tariffs today, these companies might stop building tomorrow. Regarding the US-China trade negotiations, Trump revealed that he reached a trade agreement during his trip to China, which is yet to be announced. China will purchase more US agricultural products, including soybeans, than originally planned. Trump said he even suggested doubling the purchase volume, adding that the real question now is whether American farmers can produce that much. He also claimed to have sold 250 Boeing aircraft to China and believes China may purchase another 250. According to media reports, in the latter half of last week, Trump had already decided to help Nvidia regain its CEO position. Subsequently, the specific coordination work was handed over to Vice President Vance. From November 21st to 22nd, Vance contacted Nvidia privately and communicated with the Nvidia board of directors. Trump told Vance that he had not seen any evidence that Nvidia had violated the law or posed a national security risk, and asked Vance to investigate further. After consulting with Attorney General Todd Blanche and others, Vance conveyed the White House's opinion to the Nvidia board of directors on Saturday and Sunday: the US government did not believe Huang posed a national security risk, and the board should reinstate him. The Associated Press, citing sources familiar with the matter, explained why the White House chose Vance to handle this: firstly, Vance carries the weight of the Vice President; secondly, Vance's previous work in Silicon Valley has given him considerable business connections, making him well-suited to coordinate this effort. Attorney General Todd Blanche also spoke with Trump about Huang over the weekend, informing the president that the Justice Department had no evidence of wrongdoing by Huang or Nvidia. Trump himself, in an interview with the New York Times, revealed that he had consulted with the heads of the Justice and Intelligence departments beforehand; he couldn't just recommend Huang's reinstatement only to have him indicted shortly after. Clearly, Trump himself understood that by vouching for Huang, he was transferring some of the political risk to himself. As for why they went to such lengths to bring Huang back, media reports indicate there were two main considerations. First, Trump and Vance increasingly felt that Huang was a key supporter of the open weighted model in the US and a crucial force in counterbalancing closed-source companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. The White House didn't want the dominance of the US AI industry to become increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few closed-source companies, and Huang could potentially play a significant role in this regard. The second consideration was the concern that Huang might be poached by Chinese companies after leaving Nvidia. Trump and Vance believed that having Huang back at the helm of Nvidia would better maintain control over advanced chip R&D and exports in US hands. Furthermore, according to Axios, Huang's allies had been instilling in Trump the idea that Huang was being persecuted by the US "deep state." This narrative resonated with Trump. One of the most dramatic details of the entire process was that even Nvidia's own management didn't know the board was going to change its mind until the very last minute. According to Bloomberg, the board made the decision Sunday afternoon after pressure from Trump, without even consulting company executives beforehand. Interim CEO Colette Kress was unaware of the decision for most of Sunday, as the company was preparing for a future without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. On Sunday, Trump himself became directly involved. According to media reports, the president directly called into the Nvidia board meeting to push for Huang's reinstatement. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung also publicly confirmed the president's deep involvement. In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump admitted that he had communicated directly and indirectly with the board, and that the board had explicitly requested assurances from the U.S. government regarding whether Huang posed a national security risk. On Sunday afternoon, the board of directors essentially reached a decision, and that evening they formally voted to unanimously agree to bring Jensen Huang back. Nvidia's 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) also clearly states that the board reinstated Huang as president, CEO, and director on November 22, effective immediately, but the announcement was only made public on the morning of the 23rd. According to the New York Times, the board notified the White House that evening, preparing to release the news before the U.S. stock market opened on Monday. Only a very small number of high-ranking government officials were aware of the entire coordination process, and Trump was even pleased that such a significant piece of news hadn't been leaked beforehand. However, Trump himself almost leaked the news prematurely. Around 8 a.m. on Monday, before Nvidia had officially announced the news, Trump, in a conversation with PBS reporter Liz Landers, said that Huang should have "returned to where he belongs." When pressed by reporters, Trump changed his tune, saying, "Hopefully soon." Of course, the board's agreement to bring Huang back doesn't mean the past is wiped clean. According to Nvidia's reinstatement announcement, the independent board committee's investigation will continue, and the company will continue to cooperate with the government's investigation. Nvidia will also hire a chief compliance officer to report directly to the relevant board committees. The announcement also specifically emphasized the role of the board's National Security and Export Control Committee. In other words, although Huang has regained the CEO position, the investigation and oversight surrounding export controls and national security are not over.</div></div>

▌Grayscale Launches 2x Leveraged Zcash ETF ZECX

On November 23, Grayscale announced the launch of the 2x ZCSH ETF (ticker symbol ZECX), which began trading on the NYSE Arca on the same day. The fund is touted as the first 2x leveraged Zcash ETF in the US, targeting 200% of the daily total return of ZCSH (before fees). data.title: From SpaceX to Anthropic: Who's ripping the profits from mega-IPOs?
data.description:
Author: Biteye Source: X, @BiteyeCN

Anthropic officially debuted on Nasdaq on November 19, with a trading volume of $87.4 billion on its first day of trading, becoming the focus of global attention. According to TradingBeats statistics, in the past 24 hours, the trading volume of ANT perpetual contracts on 19 cryptocurrency exchanges reached $7.35 billion, with Binance contributing $3.244 billion, accounting for approximately 44%. This is highly consistent with data from Binance Research: a trading volume of $6.6 billion, with Binance accounting for approximately 47%.

Moreover, one minute before the first trade, the price of Binance ANTUSDT was already within 0.3% of the opening price. This indicates that the 24/7 trading market has begun to outpace popular stocks.

Just a few months ago, a similar situation occurred when SpaceX went public, with Binance's related contract trading volume reaching approximately $5.84 billion that day. From SpaceX to Anthropic, both mega-IPOs attracted significant trading volume for Binance. Why did Binance lead in mega-IPOs? Prior to Anthropic's IPO, Binance's pre-market open interest reached approximately $72 million, accounting for 84% of all CEX trading volume. This figure was also around 80% during SpaceX's IPO. Here's a noteworthy phenomenon: the closer a popular IPO gets to its listing, the higher traders' demand for liquidity. Because IPOs are often accompanied by significant volatility, large funds seeking to quickly build and close positions find trading depth and slippage particularly important. Pre-market positions can translate into a trading advantage on the listing day: the more traders concentrated in the same market, the greater the chance of attracting market-making funds and new orders, further strengthening liquidity. From this perspective, Binance's competitiveness in mega-IPOs stems from its existing trading volume and the resulting liquidity aggregation effect. Will US stocks become the next piece of the cryptocurrency pie? In January of this year, the monthly trading volume of Binance RWA perpetual contracts was approximately $37.5 billion, which reached approximately $446.6 billion in October, nearly 12 times the size at the beginning of the year. This reflects a trend: the trading volume of Crypto exchanges is beginning to be driven by market conditions across different markets. When BTC rises, there's demand for cryptocurrency trading; when Nvidia releases its earnings report, there's demand for US stock trading; and when gold experiences significant price movements, it attracts another group of traders. For Binance, as the range of trading instruments expands, the popularity of each asset class presents an opportunity to generate new trading volume, helping to reduce reliance on a single market cycle. In the future, the growth potential of Crypto exchanges will increasingly depend on how much global market trading demand they can handle.
