data.title: Nvidia's computing power moves south to Johor: A two-hundred-year history of Southeast Asian landings.
data.description:
Text｜Sleepy

Johor Bahru has no mountains.

Johor Bahru is the capital of Johor, the southernmost state in Malaysia, separated from Singapore only by the Johor Strait. The highest point in the city is just a small hill, called Bukit Timbalan in Malay, and Flag Hill by the older Chinese. On the hill stands the Sultan Ibrahim Building, completed in 1940, which was formerly the Johor state government. In early 1942, the Japanese army used it as their command post for the attack on Singapore. Standing on the building and looking south, across the strait is Woodlands, the northernmost point of Singapore, with rows of government-built public housing blocks standing on the shore.

Even the name "Johor Bahru" was brought from the other side. In the Kranji area in northwestern Singapore, gambier was once widely planted. The branches and leaves of this shrub were boiled down to make a paste that could be used for tanning leather and dyeing cloth.

The older generation of Chinese called that place "Old Mountain." Later, the land ran out of nutrients, and the firewood for making oil palm oil was all cut down. So people crossed the strait and settled in Johor, which became known as Johor Bahru. One hundred and eighty years later, Old Mountain was once again completely depleted. In 2019, Singapore suspended approvals for new data centers, as land, fresh water, and electricity resources reached their limits. So people crossed the sea again. [Image of YTL Green Data Center Park entrance in Kulai, Johor | Source: Paul Mah] The two small towns of Kulai and Senai, located 30 kilometers north of Johor Bahru, where oil palm oil was once made along the riverbank, now house server rooms. Solar panels have been laid on over 1,600 acres of converted oil palm land, and the server room buildings are taller than the surrounding oil palm trees. In just over three years, Johor's data center capacity has surged from 10 megawatts to 1.3 gigawatts. According to a 2026 report by real estate consultancy Knight Frank, Johor's planned data center pipeline reaches 8,542 megawatts, ranking first in the Asia-Pacific region. The Senai Technology Park has now been incorporated into a new development area of ​​over 7,000 acres, named Ibrahim Technology City, after the Sultan of Johor, Ibrahim. At the park's opening, the president of Johor's state government investment agency explained the division of labor to the media: Johor provides land and scale, while Singapore provides capital and speed. Water is rarely absent from the naming conventions of Southeast Asian Chinese. Over a hundred years ago, those who carried silver dollars and letters back to their ancestral homes in China for Southeast Asian Chinese were called "water carriers." Singaporean water carriers typically traveled south in December with the northeast monsoon and returned north in June of the following year with the southwest monsoon. In the early years, they took a 10-20% commission, which later decreased to 3% as more people entered the trade. They didn't draw up written agreements or seek guarantors; they relied on shared hometowns and clansmanship, knowing which village your family lived in. The recipient would send a short message as a reply, often written by the smugglers. Later, the term "smuggler" specifically referred to those who carried goods across the Shenzhen River between Shenzhen and Hong Kong. For example, at the Hong Kong port of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, a private car declared as empty was stopped; its trunk contained approximately 280 kilograms of live lobsters, with 70 old professional graphics cards underneath. However, in the eyes of those in the computing power business in Singapore and Malaysia, the graphics card resale business across the Shenzhen River was just small-scale. The truly large-scale operators used a Singaporean entity to directly buy cards from upstream suppliers, transported the machines to data centers in Malaysia, used several layers of intermediary companies, and then leased the computing power to large Chinese manufacturers. According to them, for a long time, this wasn't even considered smuggling because it was legal. In February 2025, Nvidia listed Singapore separately in its financial reports for the first time. That fiscal year, revenue with invoicing addresses in Singapore amounted to $23.684 billion, accounting for 18% of total revenue; by the end of July, this proportion had risen to 22%. This city-state of over six million people once supported more than one-fifth of the chip giant's revenue. On the same page, in small print, Nvidia noted that while customers used Singapore for centralized invoicing, products were almost always shipped elsewhere; goods actually delivered to Singapore accounted for less than 2% of revenue that fiscal year. In November 2025, Nvidia switched to disclosing revenue based on customer headquarters location, and the Singapore entry disappeared from its financial reports. As for Malaysia, just across the strait, it never appeared in Nvidia's financial reports during those years. Until November 13, 2026, the Malaysian Ministry of International Trade and Industry reiterated that no permits were required to import AI chips into Malaysia; only exports and transshipments required them. Three days later, the U.S. Department of Commerce issued new regulations requiring licenses for the export of advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil.
